title: Dietary pectic glycans are degraded by coordinated enzyme pathways in human colonic Bacteroides
authors: Luis AS, Briggs J, Zhang X, Farnell B, Ndeh D, Labourel A, et al.
population: Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron and other human colonic Bacteroides species in culture; recombinant enzymes
funder: This work was supported in part by an Advanced Grant from the European Research Council (Grant No. 322820) awarded to H.J.G. and B.H., a Wellcome Trust Senior Investigator Award to HJG (grant No. WT097907MA), a European Union Seventh Framework Initial Training Network Programme entitled the WallTraC project (Grant Agreement number 263916) awarded to M-C.R. and H.J.G, and the Biotechnology and Biological Research Council project Ricefuel (BB/K020358/1) awarded to H.J.G.
authorConflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest with the contents of this article.
result: Homogalacturonan (HG) comprises alpha-1,4-linked D-galacturonic acid; B. thetaiotaomicron, a human colonic bacterium, utilises all known pectin structures through polysaccharide utilisation loci. HG-derived oligosaccharides imported into the periplasm (SusC homologue BT4114 required for growth on HG) are cleaved by endo-acting polysaccharide lyases, generating 4,5-unsaturated galacturonic acid; BT4108 (GH105) removes the unsaturated residue and the exo-alpha-galacturonidase BT4123 depolymerises the products to galacturonic acid. About 70% of the human gut Bacteroidetes tested grew on HG; wild-type B. thetaiotaomicron released pectin breakdown products that supported other Bacteroides in co-culture.
